title: Weekly Briefing: Robots Could Do 74% of Physical Work, Bricklayers Beat College Grads, and Tech Now Drives 76% of S&P 500 Earnings Growth
author: Jacob Morgan
summary: Jacob Morgan's Future Ready Leadership Weekly Briefing curates three stories and adds his own commentary for people leaders. The first covers Anthropic research finding that robots could perform 74% of physical tasks but are cost-competitive for only 0.3% of them today, which he uses to separate technical possibility from economic adoption. The second draws on The Atlantic's report of 42% underemployment among recent graduates and surging vocational enrollment, and he argues the old degree-equals-security formula needs updating rather than declaring college dead. The third summarises Andreessen Horowitz's State of Markets II, where technology supplied about 76% of S&P 500 earnings growth and investment is moving from bits to atoms. His closing observation is that few companies track an AI metric even though many claim impact. The issue also promotes a podcast episode with Jabil's CHRO.
points: Capability is not adoption: robots can do most physical tasks, yet are economically competitive for a tiny fraction, so leaders should plan for a long, uneven transition.
AI transformation will reach drivers, warehouse staff and factory workers, not only office staff using copilots.
Rising graduate underemployment and a falling college wage premium mean skills-based hiring and apprenticeship pathways deserve real investment.
Technology has become the economic cycle itself, with spending shifting toward chips, power, manufacturing and robotics.
Many companies report AI impact but few track an AI metric, a gap that leaders can close by measuring outcomes.
quotes: Headlines about automation tend to collapse capability and adoption into the same thing. A robot may be able to perform a task in a controlled warehouse or factory without being practical enough to replace the person doing it tomorrow.

Anthropic found that robots are currently cost-competitive with human labor for just 0.3% of job tasks. If robot prices continue falling at roughly their historical rate, it could take around 40 years before that reaches 10%.

AI transformation is no longer mainly about office workers using copilots. Increasingly, it will involve the people moving packages, driving vehicles, manufacturing products, cleaning facilities, and operating physical infrastructure.
I would not interpret this as “college is dead.” That is much too simplistic, but the old formula of degree equals security and trades equal limited opportunity clearly needs updating.

If companies genuinely want to move toward skills-based hiring, this is the moment to prove it. Talent may increasingly arrive through apprenticeships, vocational programs, certifications, community colleges, and alternative pathways rather than one traditional four-year route.
Nearly 30% of S&P 500 companies say AI is producing some quantifiable impact, yet only around 2% report an actual tracked AI metric.

We may be simultaneously very early in actual AI adoption and very deep into the capital investment required to support it. Technology is already reshaping markets, hiring, education, infrastructure, and work, but many of the organizational effects are still unfolding.
